questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP and how does Java implement each?
questions.title: Four Pillars of OOP in Java
questions.direct_answer: The four pillars are **Encapsulation** (hide data behind `private` + methods), **Inheritance** (acquire a parent's members via `extends`, an IS-A relationship), **Polymorphism** (one interface, many forms — overloading at compile time, overriding at runtime), and **Abstraction** (expose a contract via interfaces/abstract classes, hide the implementation). Together they keep code maintainable as it grows.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name all four pillars AND map each to its concrete Java mechanism.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting definitions without naming the Java mechanism, or confusing abstraction with encapsulation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show they interact — encapsulation makes polymorphism safe, abstraction guides inheritance boundaries — and that List<String> x = new ArrayList<>() uses all four.

sections.title: The Four Pillars of OOP — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Object-Oriented Programming organizes code around **objects** that bundle data and behavior. Java builds on four pillars, each solving a specific design problem:

- **Encapsulation** — hide internal data with `private`, expose controlled methods.
- **Inheritance** — a child class acquires a parent's members via `extends` (an IS-A relationship).
- **Polymorphism** — the same call behaves differently per object type.
- **Abstraction** — expose a contract, hide the implementation, via interfaces and abstract classes.

The goal isn't to recite them — it's to know the *mechanism* each maps to and how they reinforce each other.

sections.title: Four Pillars at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Encapsulation|~hide data|private fields|expose methods|withdraw() not setBalance()
blue|Inheritance|~IS-A via extends|child gets parent members|single inheritance only|use @Override
emerald|Polymorphism|~one interface, many forms|overloading = compile-time|overriding = runtime|JVM picks by object type
violet|Abstraction|~hide how, show what|interface = 100%|abstract class = partial|design principle

sections.title: Each Pillar in Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Definitions without mechanisms**: name the Java tool for each (`private`, `extends`, overriding, interfaces).
- **Abstraction vs encapsulation**: abstraction hides complexity; encapsulation hides data.
- **Calling overloading 'runtime polymorphism'**: overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation** → `private` fields + methods.
- **Inheritance** → `extends`, IS-A, single inheritance via classes.
- **Polymorphism** → overloading (compile-time) + overriding (runtime).
- **Abstraction** → interfaces (100%) + abstract classes (partial).
- They interact: encapsulation makes polymorphism safe; `List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()` uses all four.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: There are four pillars, and the way to answer well is to name each one and immediately tie it to the Java mechanism that implements it. The first is encapsulation. That's hiding an object's data by making the fields private and exposing controlled methods, so the class owns its own state — you call withdraw, not setBalance. The Java mechanism is the private modifier plus methods. The second is inheritance. A child class acquires the fields and methods of a parent using the extends keyword, and it models an IS-A relationship — a Dog is an Animal. Java only allows single inheritance through classes. The mechanism is extends, plus Override and super. The third is polymorphism, which means one interface, many forms. There are two kinds: overloading, which is compile-time — same method name, different parameters, and the compiler picks; and overriding, which is runtime — a parent reference pointing to a child object calls the child's version, because the JVM dispatches on the actual object type. The fourth is abstraction, which is hiding the how and exposing the what. An interface gives you a hundred percent abstraction, a pure contract, and an abstract class gives you partial abstraction. The thing that makes you stand out is showing they work together rather than as a checklist. Encapsulation is what makes polymorphism safe, because each implementation controls its own state. Abstraction guides where you draw inheritance boundaries. And one line, List of String equals new ArrayList, actually uses all four at once — List is the abstraction, ArrayList's internals are encapsulated, any List implementation substitutes via polymorphism, and ArrayList satisfies the contract through inheritance.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding in Java?
questions.title: Overloading vs Overriding — Complete Comparison
questions.direct_answer: **Overloading** is multiple methods with the **same name but different parameters** in the same class — resolved by the compiler at **compile time** (static binding). **Overriding** is a subclass redefining a parent's method with the **same signature** — resolved by the JVM at **runtime** based on the actual object (dynamic dispatch). Overloading is compile-time polymorphism; overriding is runtime polymorphism.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish compile-time vs runtime resolution and state the signature rules for each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing them up, or thinking return type alone can distinguish overloaded methods (it can't).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Override catches mistakes, overriding obeys covariant returns and can't reduce visibility, and overloading is chosen by the compiler using the reference type.

sections.title: Overloading vs Overriding — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Both are forms of polymorphism, but they happen at different times. **Overloading** means several methods share a **name** but differ in **parameter list** (count, types, or order) — within the same class. The **compiler** picks the right one based on the arguments, so it's **compile-time** (static) polymorphism.

**Overriding** means a subclass provides a new body for an inherited method with the **exact same signature**. The **JVM** picks the version based on the **actual object** at **runtime**, so it's **runtime** (dynamic) polymorphism.

A memory aid: overloading is *same name, different inputs*; overriding is *same signature, different class*.

sections.title: Overloading vs Overriding at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Overloading|~same name, diff params|same class|compiler decides|compile-time / static
blue|Overriding|~same signature|subclass redefines parent|JVM decides|runtime / dynamic
emerald|What varies|~the trigger|overloading: arguments|overriding: object type|reference vs actual type
violet|Rules|~gotchas|return type alone can't overload|@Override checks overriding|can't weaken visibility

sections.title: Overloading vs Overriding
sections.content:
| Aspect | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| **Where** | Same class | Subclass vs parent |
| **Signature** | Same name, different params | Identical signature |
| **Bound at** | Compile time (static) | Runtime (dynamic) |
| **Decided by** | Argument types | Actual object type |
| **Return type** | May differ (not enough alone) | Same or covariant |
| **Polymorphism** | Compile-time | Runtime |

sections.title: Overloading — compiler chooses by arguments
Overriding — JVM chooses by the actual object
When Each Applies
sections.content:
Use **overloading** to offer convenient variants of one operation — `print(int)`, `print(String)`, constructors with different parameter sets. It's purely a same-class API convenience.

Use **overriding** to give a subclass specialized behavior for an inherited method — the core of runtime polymorphism. Always add `@Override` so the compiler verifies you actually matched the parent signature; a tiny typo otherwise silently creates an overload instead of an override.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Overloading**: same name, different parameters, same class, compile-time.
- **Overriding**: identical signature, subclass, runtime dispatch on the actual object.
- Return type **alone** can't distinguish overloads.
- Overriding can't **weaken** visibility and must keep a same/covariant return type.
- Use `@Override` — it turns a silent mistake into a compile error.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Overloading and overriding are both polymorphism, but they happen at completely different times and that's the key distinction. Overloading is when you have multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class — different number of parameters, different types, or different order. The compiler looks at the arguments you pass and picks the matching method at compile time, which is why it's called compile-time, or static, polymorphism. A good example is a print method overloaded to take an int, a String, or two ints. One important rule: the return type alone is not enough to overload — if two methods differ only by return type, that's a compile error, because the compiler couldn't tell them apart. Overriding is different. That's when a subclass redefines a method it inherited from its parent, using the exact same signature. Here the decision is made by the JVM at runtime, based on the actual type of the object, not the type of the reference variable. So if I have an Animal reference pointing to a Dog object and I call sound, I get the Dog's version, because the JVM dispatches on the real object. That's runtime, or dynamic, polymorphism. The memory aid I use is: overloading is same name, different inputs; overriding is same signature, different class. A couple of things that make you sound careful: always put the Override annotation on overriding methods, because if you make a small typo in the signature, without the annotation Java silently treats it as a brand new overloaded method and your override never runs — with the annotation it's a compile error. And overriding has rules: you can't reduce the visibility of the method, and the return type has to be the same or a covariant subtype.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
questions.title: == vs equals() in Java
questions.direct_answer: `==` compares **references** for objects (do both point to the **same object**?) and raw values for primitives. `.equals()` compares **logical content** (are these two objects *meaningfully equal*?). For objects — especially `String` — always use `.equals()`; using `==` accidentally works sometimes (string pool, Integer cache) and fails other times, which is a classic bug.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know == is identity and .equals() is content, and why == on strings is unreliable.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Comparing strings with == and relying on the string pool making it 'work' for literals, then breaking on new String() or runtime-built values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the equals/hashCode contract: if you override equals you must override hashCode, or HashMap/HashSet break.

sections.title: == vs .equals() — Quick Overview
sections.content:
`==` and `.equals()` answer different questions. For object types, `==` asks **identity**: do these two references point to the *exact same object* in memory? `.equals()` asks **equality**: do these two objects represent the *same value*?

For **primitives** (`int`, `char`, ...), `==` simply compares the values — there are no references involved, so it's the correct tool.

The trap is `String`: literals are interned in the **string pool**, so `==` may *appear* to work for `"hi" == "hi"`. But a `new String("hi")` or a string built at runtime is a different object, and `==` returns `false`. The fix is simple — compare object content with `.equals()`.

sections.title: == vs .equals() at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|== on objects|~identity|same object?|compares references/addresses|true only if same instance
blue|== on primitives|~value compare|int, char, boolean|no references involved|correct tool here
emerald|.equals()|~content equality|same value?|default is == unless overridden|String/Integer override it
rose|String trap|~pool makes == 'work'|literals interned|new String() differs|always use .equals()

sections.title: Bug — comparing strings with ==
Fix — compare content with .equals()
== vs .equals()
sections.content:
| Aspect | `==` | `.equals()` |
|---|---|---|
| **Compares** | References (or primitive values) | Logical content |
| **Question** | Same object? | Same value? |
| **Primitives** | Correct tool | Not applicable |
| **Objects** | Identity only | Equality (if overridden) |
| **String** | Unreliable (pool-dependent) | Always correct |

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use `==` for **primitives** and for genuine **identity checks** (e.g. `if (node == head)` or `obj == null`). Use `.equals()` for comparing the **content** of objects — strings, wrappers, your own value objects.

If you write your own class and want value equality, **override `equals()` and `hashCode()` together**; otherwise the default `equals()` is just `==`, and your objects won't behave correctly as `HashMap` keys or `HashSet` elements.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `==` = identity (same object) or primitive value; `.equals()` = content equality.
- Always compare **strings** (and wrappers) with `.equals()`.
- Use `==` only for primitives, `null` checks, and deliberate identity.
- Override **`equals()` and `hashCode()` together** for value classes.
- `"literal".equals(x)` is null-safe and avoids NPEs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Double equals and the equals method answer two different questions. For objects, double equals checks identity — it asks whether two references point to the exact same object in memory. The equals method checks equality — it asks whether two objects represent the same value, the same content. For primitives like int or char there are no references, so double equals just compares the values, and that's the right tool. The classic trap is with strings. String literals are stored in something called the string pool and reused, so if you write the literal hi twice and compare with double equals, it might actually return true because both point to the same pooled object. That fools people into thinking double equals works for strings. But the moment you do new String of hi, or you build a string at runtime from user input, you get a different object, and double equals returns false even though the text is identical. So the rule is: always compare strings, and wrapper objects, with the equals method, never double equals. A neat trick is to call equals on the literal — admin dot equals of user — because that's also null-safe; if user is null you get false instead of a NullPointerException. The thing that makes you stand out is mentioning the equals and hashCode contract. If you write your own class and override equals to compare by value, you must also override hashCode, and in a consistent way — equal objects must have equal hash codes. If you override one and not the other, your objects will misbehave as keys in a HashMap or elements in a HashSet, because those collections use hashCode to find the bucket and equals to confirm the match.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
questions.title: Abstract Class vs Interface — Full Comparison
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract class** can hold **state** (instance fields), **constructors**, and a mix of concrete and abstract methods, but a class can extend **only one**. An **interface** is a pure **contract** — no instance state, and a class can implement **many**. Use an abstract class for a shared base with common code/state; use an interface to define a capability multiple unrelated types can have.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the concrete capability differences and the design trade-off (single inheritance vs multiple).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'interfaces can't have method bodies' (false since Java 8 default methods) or forgetting interfaces can't hold instance state.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame it as IS-A shared base (abstract class) vs CAN-DO capability (interface), and note interfaces enable multiple inheritance of type.

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Both define abstract types you can't instantiate directly, but they differ in capability. An **abstract class** is a partially built base: it can have **instance fields** (state), **constructors**, and both concrete and abstract methods — but a class can `extends` only **one**.

An **interface** is a **contract**. Since Java 8 it can carry `default`/`static` method bodies, but it still has **no instance state** and **no constructors**, and a class can `implements` **many**.

The design rule of thumb: abstract class models an **IS-A** with shared implementation; interface models a **CAN-DO** capability that even unrelated types can share.

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Abstract class|~partial base|instance fields + constructors|concrete + abstract methods|extend only ONE
blue|Interface|~contract|no instance state|default/static methods (Java 8+)|implement MANY
emerald|Inheritance|~the big trade-off|single via classes|multiple via interfaces|interfaces avoid diamond on state
violet|Design choice|~IS-A vs CAN-DO|abstract = shared base|interface = capability|unrelated types can share

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface
sections.content:
| Aspect | Abstract Class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| **Instance state** | Yes (fields) | No (only constants) |
| **Constructors** | Yes | No |
| **Methods** | Concrete + abstract | Abstract + default/static/private |
| **Inheritance** | Extend one | Implement many |
| **Keyword** | `extends` | `implements` |
| **Models** | IS-A shared base | CAN-DO capability |

sections.title: Abstract class — shared state + partial implementation
sections.content:
```java
abstract class Employee {
    private final String name;        // state — only an abstract class can hold this
    Employee(String name) { this.name = name; } // constructor
    String getName() { return name; }            // concrete shared method
    abstract double pay();                        // subclasses differ
}
```

sections.title: Interface — a capability many types can implement
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Choose an **abstract class** when subclasses are clearly the same *kind* of thing and need to **share state and code** — a common base with a template method.

Choose an **interface** when you're defining a **capability** that types may have regardless of their hierarchy (`Comparable`, `Runnable`, `Serializable`), or when a type needs to play **multiple roles**. Since you can implement many interfaces but extend one class, interfaces are also how Java gives you multiple inheritance of *type*.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Abstract class: **state + constructors + concrete code**, extend **one**.
- Interface: **no instance state**, `default`/`static` methods allowed, implement **many**.
- Interfaces give multiple inheritance of **type**; classes give single inheritance.
- Abstract class = **IS-A** shared base; interface = **CAN-DO** capability.
- Since Java 8, 'interfaces have no bodies' is outdated — default methods exist.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Both an abstract class and an interface define a type you can't instantiate directly, but they have different capabilities and they signal different design intent. An abstract class is like a partially built base class. It can have instance fields, so it can hold state. It can have constructors. And it can mix concrete methods, which carry shared implementation, with abstract methods that subclasses must fill in. The big limitation is that a class can only extend one abstract class, because Java has single inheritance for classes. An interface is a contract. Since Java 8 it can actually carry method bodies through default and static methods, so the old line that interfaces can't have implementations is outdated. But an interface still can't hold instance state and has no constructors. The advantage is that a class can implement as many interfaces as it wants. So the design rule of thumb I use is: an abstract class models an IS-A relationship with shared implementation — these things are fundamentally the same kind of thing and share code and state. An interface models a CAN-DO capability — it says this type can do something, and even completely unrelated types can implement the same interface. Comparable, Runnable, Serializable are all capabilities. And because you can implement many interfaces but extend only one class, interfaces are how Java gives you multiple inheritance of type without the diamond problem you'd get from multiple inheritance of state. So practically: if subclasses need to share fields and concrete code, reach for an abstract class. If you're defining a capability, or a type needs to play several roles, use interfaces.

questions.question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in Java?
questions.title: Composition vs Inheritance in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** is an **IS-A** relationship (`Dog extends Animal`) — a subclass reuses a parent's implementation, but it's tight coupling fixed at compile time. **Composition** is a **HAS-A** relationship (`Car has an Engine`) — an object holds other objects and delegates to them, giving flexible, swappable behavior. The widely-taught guideline is **prefer composition over inheritance**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the IS-A vs HAS-A test and why composition is usually the safer default.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for inheritance just to reuse code, creating fragile deep hierarchies and breaking the IS-A test.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the fragile base class problem and that composition lets you swap behavior at runtime (strategy pattern).

sections.title: Composition vs Inheritance — Quick Overview
sections.content:
**Inheritance** expresses **IS-A**: `Dog extends Animal` means a dog *is an* animal and inherits its implementation. It's powerful but **tightly coupled** — the subclass depends on the parent's internals, the relationship is fixed at compile time, and Java allows only one parent.

**Composition** expresses **HAS-A**: a `Car` *has an* `Engine` — it holds a reference to another object and **delegates** work to it. You can swap that part, even at runtime, and combine many pieces freely.

The famous guideline (from *Effective Java*) is **prefer composition over inheritance**: use inheritance only when the IS-A test genuinely holds; otherwise compose.

sections.title: Composition vs Inheritance at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Inheritance|~IS-A|Dog extends Animal|reuse parent implementation|tight coupling, compile-time
blue|Composition|~HAS-A|Car has an Engine|hold + delegate|loose coupling, swappable
emerald|The test|~which to use|IS-A true -> extends|HAS-A true -> compose|when unsure, compose
violet|Why prefer composition|~flexibility|swap behavior at runtime|avoid fragile base class|combine many parts

sections.title: Composition vs Inheritance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| **Relationship** | IS-A | HAS-A |
| **Coupling** | Tight | Loose |
| **Flexibility** | Fixed at compile time | Swappable at runtime |
| **Reuse via** | `extends` parent | Holding + delegating |
| **Limit** | One parent class | Compose many parts |
| **Risk** | Fragile base class | A bit more boilerplate |

sections.title: Inheritance misused for reuse
Composition — hold and delegate
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **inheritance** only when the **IS-A** test truly holds and you want subclasses to be substitutable for the parent (Liskov) — e.g. `Circle extends Shape`.

Use **composition** for everything else: reusing code without an IS-A relationship, combining multiple behaviors, or wanting to swap an implementation at runtime (the strategy pattern). When in doubt, compose — it avoids the fragile base class problem, where a change in the parent silently breaks subclasses.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Inheritance = **IS-A** (`extends`); composition = **HAS-A** (hold + delegate).
- Inheritance is tight coupling fixed at compile time; composition is loose and swappable.
- Run the **IS-A test** first; if it fails, compose.
- Guideline: **prefer composition over inheritance** (avoids fragile base class).
- Composition enables runtime behavior swapping (strategy pattern).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Inheritance and composition are two ways to reuse code, and the difference is the relationship they express. Inheritance is an IS-A relationship. Dog extends Animal means a dog is an animal, and it inherits the parent's implementation. It's powerful, but it's tight coupling — the subclass depends on the parent's internals, the relationship is fixed at compile time, and in Java you only get one parent class. Composition is a HAS-A relationship. A Car has an Engine — the car holds a reference to an engine object and delegates work to it. The advantage is flexibility: you can swap that part out, even at runtime, and you can combine lots of pieces together freely. The test I run before choosing is simple: does IS-A genuinely hold? A dog really is an animal, so inheritance fits. But a queue is not a stack, even if a stack happens to have the methods I want to reuse — so I shouldn't extend Stack just to borrow its methods. If I do, I leak the entire Stack API and callers can break my queue's semantics. Instead I compose: my Queue holds a Deque privately and delegates enqueue and dequeue to it, exposing only the operations I want. The well-known guideline, from Effective Java, is prefer composition over inheritance. The reason is the fragile base class problem — with inheritance, a change in the parent class can silently break all the subclasses, because they're so tightly bound to its implementation. Composition avoids that, and it's what lets you implement patterns like strategy, where you inject different behavior at runtime. So: use inheritance only when IS-A really holds and subclasses are substitutable for the parent; otherwise, compose.

beats.text: **Inheritance** (IS-A) creates a parent-child class hierarchy — the subclass inherits the parent's implementation, creating **tight coupling**.

items: **Composition** (HAS-A) builds objects by including references to other objects
more **flexible** because you can swap implementations at runtime and avoid deep hierarchies. The classic advice is 'favor composition over inheritance.'

questions.question: How do the four OOP principles work together in a real Java application?
questions.title: OOP Principles Working Together in Java
questions.direct_answer: In a real app the pillars combine: **abstraction** defines a `PaymentProcessor` interface, concrete classes use **inheritance** (`implements`) to fulfill it, each keeps its data **encapsulated** (private fields), and the service calls them through **polymorphism** (one reference, runtime dispatch). The result: adding a new payment type is a new class with **zero edits** to existing code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can show the four pillars cooperating in one cohesive design, not as isolated definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating the pillars as a disconnected checklist instead of showing how they reinforce each other in a feature.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie it to the Open/Closed Principle: abstraction + polymorphism let you extend behavior without modifying existing, tested code.

sections.title: How the Four Pillars Work Together — Quick Overview
sections.content:
In real code the pillars aren't separate features — they reinforce each other. Take a checkout system. **Abstraction** sets the contract: a `PaymentProcessor` interface with `process(Order)`. **Inheritance** lets `CardProcessor` and `UpiProcessor` `implements` that contract. **Encapsulation** keeps each processor's secrets (card number, API key) private. **Polymorphism** lets the `CheckoutService` hold a `PaymentProcessor` reference and call `process()` without knowing the concrete type — the JVM dispatches at runtime.

The payoff is the **Open/Closed Principle**: adding ApplePay means writing one new class. No existing, tested code changes.

sections.title: Pillars in One Feature
sections.content:
amber|Abstraction|~the contract|PaymentProcessor interface|process(Order)|callers depend on this
blue|Inheritance|~fulfill the contract|CardProcessor implements it|UpiProcessor implements it|code reuse via base
emerald|Encapsulation|~hide secrets|private cardNumber|private apiKey|validate internally
violet|Polymorphism|~runtime dispatch|one reference, many types|add ApplePay = new class|Open/Closed Principle

sections.title: All Four Pillars in a Checkout Flow
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checklist thinking**: listing pillars separately instead of showing them cooperate in one design.
- **Skipping encapsulation in implementations**: a processor that exposes its API key undermines the whole design.
- **Switch on type instead of polymorphism**: `if (type == CARD)...` reintroduces the edits abstraction was meant to remove.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstraction** defines the contract (`PaymentProcessor`).
- **Inheritance** (`implements`) lets concrete types fulfill it.
- **Encapsulation** hides each implementation's private state.
- **Polymorphism** dispatches at runtime through one reference.
- Together they deliver the **Open/Closed Principle**: extend by adding classes, not editing existing ones.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The best way to answer this is to walk through one real feature and show the pillars reinforcing each other, rather than listing them separately. Take a checkout system that supports multiple payment methods. It starts with abstraction: I define a PaymentProcessor interface with a single process method that takes an order. That's the contract — it says what a payment processor can do without saying how. Then inheritance comes in: concrete classes like CardProcessor and UpiProcessor implement that interface, and they can share common code through a base class if needed. Each of those classes uses encapsulation — a CardProcessor keeps its API key and card details in private fields and validates them internally, so its secrets never leak. Finally, polymorphism ties it together. My CheckoutService holds a PaymentProcessor reference and just calls process. It has no idea whether it's talking to a card processor or a UPI processor; the JVM dispatches to the right one at runtime based on the actual object. Now here's the payoff, and this is the part that impresses interviewers: this design follows the Open/Closed Principle. When the business says we now support Apple Pay, I write one new class, ApplePayProcessor, that implements the interface. I don't touch the CheckoutService, I don't touch the existing processors, I don't edit any tested code. Compare that to the naive version with a big if-else or switch on a payment-type enum — every new method forces you to edit and retest that central method. So the four pillars working together is exactly what lets you extend a system by adding code instead of modifying existing code.
